title: Antenatal screening programmes and ethical choices
blurb: Time and explain the FASP, SCT and IDPS tests, interpret a higher-chance result, describe NIPT and diagnostic options, and support a free, informed choice.
question: Grace, 39, has a combined test result giving a 1 in 80 chance of Down's syndrome. She asks: 'Does this mean my baby has it?' How should the midwife explain the result and her options?

teach.body: A screening test sorts people into higher and lower chance groups; it does not tell a woman whether her baby has a condition. A diagnostic test gives a definite answer. In the NHS, every screening test is offered so that each woman can make a personal informed choice, and she may accept or decline any part of any programme. In plain English: screening answers 'how likely?', diagnosis answers 'yes or no?'.
teach.cite: NHS FASP, SCT and IDPS overviews; NICE NG201 1.2.13

teach.body: Screening can lead to hard decisions, so the midwife gives balanced information before each test, checks understanding, and supports whatever the woman decides, even if it differs from the professional's view (NICE NG201 1.3.3). Declining is a valid choice and does not change her right to care. Unexpected results lead to prompt referral with information and support. SPM 3.20 expects midwives to understand the ethical dilemmas screening can raise.

The midwife explains that 1 in 80 falls in the higher chance group (1 in 2 to 1 in 150), which means 79 in 80 women with this result have a baby without Down's syndrome. It is not a diagnosis. Grace's options are NIPT (a further screen), a diagnostic test (CVS or amniocentesis), or no further testing. The midwife gives time and written information, avoids steering, and respects Grace's decision.

teach.text: In 'chance' results, a SMALLER second number means a HIGHER chance: 1 in 80 is higher than 1 in 150, and 1 in 1,000 is lower. And NIPT is screening, not diagnosis: a higher chance NIPT still needs CVS or amniocentesis to confirm.

items: Screening gives a chance; diagnostic tests (CVS, amniocentesis) give a definite answer.
Combined test (10+0 to 14+1) screens for T21, T18 and T13; quadruple test (to 20+0) for T21.
20-week scan at 18+0 to 20+6 (complete by 23+0) screens for T18, T13 and 9 physical conditions.
Higher chance is 1 in 2 to 1 in 150; NIPT is then offered, alongside diagnostic testing.
SCT: blood test (high prevalence) or family origin questionnaire (low); thalassaemia for all; father tested if she is a carrier.
Every test is a free, informed choice; respect her decision and keep supporting her.

summary: You can now explain the difference between screening and diagnosis, time the combined, quadruple and 20-week tests, and interpret a higher-chance result with NIPT and diagnostic options. You can also run SCT screening and support a woman's informed choice without steering her.

A.q: Which conditions does the first-trimester combined test assess the chance of?
A.why: FASP: the combined test assesses the chance of Down's (T21), Edwards' (T18) and Patau's (T13) syndromes and is the test of choice.

whyNot.0: Spina bifida is screened at the 20-week scan.
whyNot.2: The combined test includes Down's syndrome too.
whyNot.3: Cystic fibrosis is screened for on the newborn blood spot.

A.q: A woman books too late for the combined test. Which condition does the second-trimester quadruple test screen for?
A.why: FASP: the quadruple test is offered in the second trimester to assess the chance of Down's syndrome.

whyNot.0: Edwards' screening runs to 14+1 (combined) or via the 20-week scan.
whyNot.1: Patau's screening runs to 14+1 (combined) or via the 20-week scan.
whyNot.3: Spina bifida is screened at the 20-week scan.

A.q: Within which window is the 20-week fetal anomaly scan offered?
A.why: FASP and NG201 1.2.15: 18+0 to 20+6 weeks, and it can be completed up to 23+0.

whyNot.0: This is earlier than the programme window.
whyNot.2: This starts later than the programme window.
whyNot.3: This is the dating scan window.

B.q: Which combined test result is classed as higher chance, so that NIPT is offered?
B.why: FASP: NIPT is offered after a higher chance result between 1 in 2 and 1 in 150; 1 in 100 is within that range.

whyNot.0: 1 in 200 is a lower chance than 1 in 150.
whyNot.1: 1 in 500 is a lower chance result.
whyNot.2: 1 in 1,000 is a lower chance result.

B.q: In a low prevalence area, how is it decided which pregnant women are offered a blood test for sickle cell disease?
B.why: SCT: in low prevalence areas a family origin questionnaire identifies women likely to be carriers; in high prevalence areas all women have a blood test.

whyNot.1: Fathers are offered testing after the woman is found to be a carrier.
whyNot.2: The heel prick is newborn screening, not antenatal.
whyNot.3: A scan cannot detect haemoglobin disorders.

B.q: Antenatal screening shows that Adaeze is a carrier of sickle cell. What should be offered next?
B.why: SCT: all biological fathers are offered screening if the woman is a carrier, to find out the baby's chance of an inherited disorder.

whyNot.0: Diagnostic testing is not the next step for a carrier; the father's result shows first whether the baby is at risk.
whyNot.2: Repeating her result adds nothing; the father's status is needed.
whyNot.3: Waiting until birth removes the chance of an informed antenatal choice.

C.q: Grace, 39, has a combined test result of 1 in 80 for Down's syndrome and asks if her baby has it. Which response is most accurate?
options: Yes: a result above 1 in 150 confirms it
No: below 1 in 150 means a lower chance
Yes, unless the 20-week scan is normal
No: it is a screen, not a diagnosis
C.why: 1 in 80 is a higher chance result (1 in 2 to 1 in 150), not a diagnosis. She can choose NIPT, CVS or amniocentesis, or no further testing.

whyNot.0: Screening never confirms a diagnosis; CVS or amniocentesis is needed.
whyNot.1: 1 in 80 is a higher chance than 1 in 150, not a lower one.
whyNot.2: A normal scan does not rule out Down's syndrome.

C.q: After full discussion, Grace decides not to have NIPT or any diagnostic test. What should the midwife do?
options: Advise that NIPT is needed for birth planning
Respect her decision and continue her care
Refer her to a consultant to reconsider
Book an amniocentesis in case she changes her mind
C.why: Each screening and diagnostic test is a choice; NICE NG201 1.3.3 says women's decisions should be respected even when contrary to the professional's view.

whyNot.0: Further testing is optional and not required for birth planning.
whyNot.2: Referral to change her mind is pressure, not support.
whyNot.3: Booking a test she has declined disregards her choice.

C.q: Maya first books at 16 weeks. Which trisomy screening can still be offered?
options: The combined test for all three trisomies
NIPT as her first screening test
The quadruple test for Down's syndrome
No screening, as the window has passed
C.why: Down's syndrome screening runs from 10+0 to 20+0 weeks; after 14+1 the quadruple test is used. Edwards' and Patau's are then screened at the 20-week scan.

whyNot.0: The combined test window closes at 14+1.
whyNot.1: In the NHS, NIPT follows a higher chance result; it is not the first screen.
whyNot.3: Down's screening is available until 20+0 weeks.

reteach.title: Chance, then certainty, then choice
reteach.question: What three ideas sit behind every screening conversation?

blocks.body: CHANCE: screening (combined, quadruple, NIPT, scan) gives a likelihood. CERTAINTY: only CVS or amniocentesis gives a definite answer. CHOICE: every step, including no test at all, is the woman's decision, and the midwife supports it without steering.

blocks.text: The smaller the second number, the higher the chance.

explain.body: Screening tests (combined, quadruple, NIPT, scans) give a chance. Diagnostic tests (CVS, amniocentesis) give a definite answer.

test.q: Which of these is a diagnostic test?
test.why: CVS and amniocentesis are the diagnostic tests offered after a higher chance result or unexpected scan finding.

whyNot.1: The combined test is a screening test.
whyNot.3: The quadruple test is a screening test.

explain.body: Combined test 10+0 to 14+1 (T21, T18, T13). Quadruple test up to 20+0 (T21). 20-week scan 18+0 to 20+6, complete by 23+0.

test.q: Up to what gestation is screening for Edwards' and Patau's syndromes by the combined test available?
test.why: FASP: screening for Edwards' and Patau's syndromes takes place between 10+0 and 14+1 weeks.

whyNot.1: 16 weeks is after the window closes.
whyNot.2: 20+0 is the end of the Down's screening window.
whyNot.3: 12+0 is within, not the end of, the window.

explain.body: A result between 1 in 2 and 1 in 150 is higher chance. NIPT is offered as a further screen, alongside the option of CVS or amniocentesis, or no further test.

test.q: What is the higher chance range that leads to an offer of NIPT?
test.why: FASP: NIPT is offered after a higher chance result between 1 in 2 and 1 in 150.

whyNot.0: Results below 1 in 150 are lower chance.
whyNot.1: This range is mostly lower chance results.
whyNot.3: The cut-off is 1 in 150, not 1 in 500.

explain.body: Sickle cell screening: blood test for all in high prevalence areas, family origin questionnaire in low; thalassaemia offered to all; father offered testing if she is a carrier. Every test is her choice.

test.q: Which haemoglobin disorder is screening offered for in ALL pregnant women, whatever the area's prevalence?
test.why: SCT: all pregnant women are offered screening for thalassaemia; sickle cell screening depends on area prevalence (blood test or family origin questionnaire).

whyNot.1: In low prevalence areas, the family origin questionnaire decides who has the sickle cell blood test.
whyNot.2: Haemophilia is not part of SCT screening.
whyNot.3: G6PD deficiency is not part of SCT screening.
